Data Management" author: "Joe Nese" institute: "jnese@uoregon.edu" format: revealjs: theme: default highlight-style: github incremental: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 3.5 scrollable: true slide-number: true embed-resources: true execute: echo: true warning: false embed-resources: true --- ## Agenda - Tidy data - Naming stuff - Miscellany ## About me {.scrollable .smaller} - husband, dad - BA, Psychology: UC Santa Barbara - PhD, School Psychology: University of Maryland - UO since 2009 at Behavioral Research & Teaching ([BRT](http://brtprojects.org)) - Research Professor **Research** - Applied statistical methods used by researchers - Developing and improving systems that support data-based decision making using advanced technologies to influence teachers' instructional practices and increase student achievement - [CORE](https://jnese.github.io/core-blog/) and [CORE II](https://jnese.github.io/coreprosody) - Inclusive Skill-building Learning Approach ([ISLA](https://www.neselab.org/isla/)) **Teaching** - Introduction to Data Science with `R` - Functional Programming for Educational Data Science - Applied Machine Learning for Educational Data Scientists - Data Science Capstone ## Data cleaning > “It is often said that 80% of data analysis is spent on the process of cleaning and preparing the data (Dasu & Johnson, 2003).” > - Hadley Wickham (Tidy Data) . . . * Persistent and varied challenge * Little research on how to do it well # Tidy Data ## Tidy Data {.smaller} 1. Each variable must have its own column 2. Each observation must have its own row 3. Each value must have its own cell . . . These three rules are interrelated because it’s impossible to only satisfy two of the three ![](https://d33wubrfki0l68.cloudfront.net/6f1ddb544fc5c69a2478e444ab8112fb0eea23f8/91adc/images/tidy-1.png) ::: aside [R4DS](https://r4ds.had.co.nz/tidy-data.html) ::: ## ![](https://cdn.myportfolio.com/45214904-6a61-4e23-98d6-b140f8654a40/85520b8f-4629-4763-8a2a-9ceff27458bf_rw_1920.jpg?h=21007b20ac00cf37318dca645c215453) ::: aside [Allison Horst](https://allisonhorst.com/other-r-fun) ::: ## ![](https://cdn.myportfolio.com/45214904-6a61-4e23-98d6-b140f8654a40/6e297111-efb7-4555-93d2-085071d1853c_rw_1920.jpg?h=f1951b118eaddaaab8a572422bc16566) ::: aside [Allison Horst](https://allisonhorst.com/other-r-fun) ::: ## Common ways data are "messy" * Column headers are values, not variable names * Multiple variables stored in one column * Variables are stored in both rows and columns * See the pivoting [vignette](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/articles/pivot.html) for examples and solutions ## Why tidy? {.smaller} A ~~biased~~ principled approach ::: {.incremental} - There are many reasons why you might want to have "messy" data - **But**... - If you have a consistent data structure, it’s easier to learn tools that work with it because the data has an underlying uniformity - There’s a specific advantage to placing variables in columns because it allows R’s vectorised nature to be optimized - Tidy data is an **extremely** useful format generally, and particularly useful when applying tools within the `{tidyverse}` - All packages within the `{tidyverse}` are designed to either help you get your data in a tidy format, or assume your data are already in a tidy format - Assuming a common data format leads to **huge** jumps in efficiency, as the output from certain functions can be directly input into others ::: ## ![](https://cdn.myportfolio.com/45214904-6a61-4e23-98d6-b140f8654a40/fc9b748b-db96-4ed4-aa23-f6e0ffc866ee_rw_1920.jpg?h=8fa394b572089354aa87b1d602b0f887) ::: aside [Allison Horst](https://allisonhorst.com/other-r-fun) ::: ## Messy data \#1 What makes this data messy? Or, why is this data not tidy? . . . ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 18 × 11 religion `<$10k` `$10-20k` `$20-30k` `$30-40k` `$40-50k` `$50-75k` `$75-100k` 1 Agnostic 27 34 60 81 76 137 122 2 Atheist 12 27 37 52 35 70 73 3 Buddhist 27 21 30 34 33 58 62 4 Catholic 418 617 732 670 638 1116 949 5 Don’t k… 15 14 15 11 10 35 21 6 Evangel… 575 869 1064 982 881 1486 949 7 Hindu 1 9 7 9 11 34 47 8 Histori… 228 244 236 238 197 223 131 9 Jehovah… 20 27 24 24 21 30 15 10 Jewish 19 19 25 25 30 95 69 11 Mainlin… 289 495 619 655 651 1107 939 12 Mormon 29 40 48 51 56 112 85 13 Muslim 6 7 9 10 9 23 16 14 Orthodox 13 17 23 32 32 47 38 15 Other C… 9 7 11 13 13 14 18 16 Other F… 20 33 40 46 49 63 46 17 Other W… 5 2 3 4 2 7 3 18 Unaffil… 217 299 374 365 341 528 407 # ℹ 3 more variables: `$100-150k` , `>150k` , # `Don't know/refused` ``` ::: ::: ## Messy data \#2 What makes this data messy? ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 7,240 × 60 country iso2 iso3 year new_sp_m_014 new_sp_m_1524 new_sp_m_2534 1 Afghanistan AF AFG 1980 NA NA NA 2 Afghanistan AF AFG 1981 NA NA NA 3 Afghanistan AF AFG 1982 NA NA NA 4 Afghanistan AF AFG 1983 NA NA NA 5 Afghanistan AF AFG 1984 NA NA NA 6 Afghanistan AF AFG 1985 NA NA NA 7 Afghanistan AF AFG 1986 NA NA NA 8 Afghanistan AF AFG 1987 NA NA NA 9 Afghanistan AF AFG 1988 NA NA NA 10 Afghanistan AF AFG 1989 NA NA NA # ℹ 7,230 more rows # ℹ 53 more variables: new_sp_m_3544 , new_sp_m_4554 , # new_sp_m_5564 , new_sp_m_65 , new_sp_f_014 , # new_sp_f_1524 , new_sp_f_2534 , new_sp_f_3544 , # new_sp_f_4554 , new_sp_f_5564 , new_sp_f_65 , # new_sn_m_014 , new_sn_m_1524 , new_sn_m_2534 , # new_sn_m_3544 , new_sn_m_4554 , new_sn_m_5564 , … ``` ::: ::: ## Messy data \#2 There are many variables in column names ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 7,240 × 60 country iso2 iso3 year new_sp_m_014 new_sp_m_1524 new_sp_m_2534 1 Afghanistan AF AFG 1980 NA NA NA 2 Afghanistan AF AFG 1981 NA NA NA 3 Afghanistan AF AFG 1982 NA NA NA 4 Afghanistan AF AFG 1983 NA NA NA 5 Afghanistan AF AFG 1984 NA NA NA 6 Afghanistan AF AFG 1985 NA NA NA 7 Afghanistan AF AFG 1986 NA NA NA 8 Afghanistan AF AFG 1987 NA NA NA 9 Afghanistan AF AFG 1988 NA NA NA 10 Afghanistan AF AFG 1989 NA NA NA # ℹ 7,230 more rows # ℹ 53 more variables: new_sp_m_3544 , new_sp_m_4554 , # new_sp_m_5564 , new_sp_m_65 , new_sp_f_014 , # new_sp_f_1524 , new_sp_f_2534 , new_sp_f_3544 , # new_sp_f_4554 , new_sp_f_5564 , new_sp_f_65 , # new_sn_m_014 , new_sn_m_1524 , new_sn_m_2534 , # new_sn_m_3544 , new_sn_m_4554 , new_sn_m_5564 , … ``` ::: ::: ## Messy data \#2 There are many variables in column names :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.fragment} Example column names ::: ::: {.fragment} [new_]{style='color:#D55E00'}[sp_]{style='color:#009E73'}[m_]{style='color:#0072B2'}[014]{style='color:#CC79A7'} [new_]{style='color:#D55E00'}[rel_]{style='color:#009E73'}[f_]{style='color:#0072B2'}[65]{style='color:#CC79A7'} ::: ::: ::: {.column width="60%" .fragment} ::: {.fragment} all `col` names start with [new_]{style='color:#D55E00'}, which we don't really need ::: ::: {.fragment} followed by a diagnosis category: ["sp" "sn" "ep" "rel"]{style='color:#009E73'} ::: ::: {.fragment} then [gender]{style='color:#0072B2'}, which in these data are limited to ["m"]{style='color:#0072B2'} or ["f"]{style='color:#0072B2'} ::: ::: {.fragment} and last an [age range]{style='color:#CC79A7'} ::: ::: {.fragment} and these are separated by underscores `_` which is actually quite convenient ::: ::: :::: . . . That's a lot of information in the column names! ## Let's tidy it . . . ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 76,046 × 8 country iso2 iso3 year diagnosis sex age_range count 1 Afghanistan AF AFG 1997 sp m 014 0 2 Afghanistan AF AFG 1997 sp m 1524 10 3 Afghanistan AF AFG 1997 sp m 2534 6 4 Afghanistan AF AFG 1997 sp m 3544 3 5 Afghanistan AF AFG 1997 sp m 4554 5 6 Afghanistan AF AFG 1997 sp m 5564 2 7 Afghanistan AF AFG 1997 sp m 65 0 8 Afghanistan AF AFG 1997 sp f 014 5 9 Afghanistan AF AFG 1997 sp f 1524 38 10 Afghanistan AF AFG 1997 sp f 2534 36 # ℹ 76,036 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Messy data \#3 What makes this data messy? ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 7 family name_child1 dob_child1 name_child2 dob_child2 name_child3 dob_child3 1 1 Susan 1998-11-26 Jose 2000-01-29 Alice 2001-02-19 2 2 Mark 1996-06-22 NA NA 3 3 Sam 2002-07-11 Seth 2004-04-05 NA 4 4 Craig 2004-10-10 Khai 2009-08-27 NA 5 5 Parker 2000-12-05 Gracie 2005-02-28 Peter 2002-05-05 ``` ::: ::: ## Messy data \#3 There are multiple observations per row ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 7 family name_child1 dob_child1 name_child2 dob_child2 name_child3 dob_child3 1 1 Susan 1998-11-26 Jose 2000-01-29 Alice 2001-02-19 2 2 Mark 1996-06-22 NA NA 3 3 Sam 2002-07-11 Seth 2004-04-05 NA 4 4 Craig 2004-10-10 Khai 2009-08-27 NA 5 5 Parker 2000-12-05 Gracie 2005-02-28 Peter 2002-05-05 ``` ::: ::: . . . We have two pieces of information (or values) for each child - `name` and `dob` These need to go into separate columns ## Tidy it up! ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 11 × 4 family child name dob 1 1 child1 Susan 1998-11-26 2 1 child2 Jose 2000-01-29 3 1 child3 Alice 2001-02-19 4 2 child1 Mark 1996-06-22 5 3 child1 Sam 2002-07-11 6 3 child2 Seth 2004-04-05 7 4 child1 Craig 2004-10-10 8 4 child2 Khai 2009-08-27 9 5 child1 Parker 2000-12-05 10 5 child2 Gracie 2005-02-28 11 5 child3 Peter 2002-05-05 ``` ::: ::: ## Let’s look at some education data ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 35 × 20 stu_name gender item_1 item_2 item_3 item_4 item_5 item_6 item_7 item_8 1 Adam M 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 0 2 Anne F 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 3 Audrey F 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 4 Barbara F 1 1 1 1 0 0 1 0 5 Bert M 1 1 1 1 1 0 1 0 6 Betty F 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 7 Blaise M 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 8 Brenda F 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 9 Britton F 1 1 1 0 1 1 1 1 10 Carol F 1 1 1 1 0 0 1 0 # ℹ 25 more rows # ℹ 10 more variables: item_9 , item_10 , item_11 , # item_12 , item_13 , item_14 , item_15 , item_16 , # item_17 , item_18 ``` ::: ::: ## Let's Discuss * Are these data tidy? * If not, what needs to happen to make them tidy? * What are the variables? What are the values? ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 35 × 20 stu_name gender item_1 item_2 item_3 item_4 item_5 item_6 item_7 item_8 1 Adam M 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 0 2 Anne F 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 3 Audrey F 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 4 Barbara F 1 1 1 1 0 0 1 0 5 Bert M 1 1 1 1 1 0 1 0 6 Betty F 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 7 Blaise M 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 8 Brenda F 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 9 Britton F 1 1 1 0 1 1 1 1 10 Carol F 1 1 1 1 0 0 1 0 # ℹ 25 more rows # ℹ 10 more variables: item_9 , item_10 , item_11 , # item_12 , item_13 , item_14 , item_15 , item_16 , # item_17 , item_18 ``` ::: ::: ## exam1 data What do we want? . . . Let’s change all `item_#` variables into two variables - `item` and `score` . . . ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 35 × 20 stu_name gender item_1 item_2 item_3 item_4 item_5 item_6 item_7 item_8 1 Adam M 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 0 2 Anne F 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 3 Audrey F 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 4 Barbara F 1 1 1 1 0 0 1 0 5 Bert M 1 1 1 1 1 0 1 0 6 Betty F 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 7 Blaise M 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 8 Brenda F 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 9 Britton F 1 1 1 0 1 1 1 1 10 Carol F 1 1 1 1 0 0 1 0 # ℹ 25 more rows # ℹ 10 more variables: item_9 , item_10 , item_11 , # item_12 , item_13 , item_14 , item_15 , item_16 , # item_17 , item_18 ``` ::: ::: ## exam1 data What do we want? Let’s change all `item_#` variables into two variables - `item` and `score` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 630 × 4 stu_name gender item score 1 Adam M 1 1 2 Adam M 2 1 3 Adam M 3 1 4 Adam M 4 1 5 Adam M 5 1 6 Adam M 6 1 7 Adam M 7 1 8 Adam M 8 0 9 Adam M 9 0 10 Adam M 10 0 # ℹ 620 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Why are tidy data useful? Easy to calculate the `prop`ortion of students responding correctly to each item . . . ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 18 × 2 item prop 1 1 1 2 2 1 3 3 1 4 4 0.914 5 5 0.886 6 6 0.857 7 7 0.886 8 8 0.771 9 9 0.857 10 10 0.686 11 11 0.343 12 12 0.171 13 13 0.2 14 14 0.0857 15 15 0.0286 16 16 0.0286 17 17 0.0286 18 18 0 ``` ::: ::: ## Why are tidy data useful? Easy to calculate the `prop`ortion correct for each item by gender . . . ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 36 × 3 # Groups: item [18] item gender prop 1 1 F 1 2 1 M 1 3 2 F 1 4 2 M 1 5 3 F 1 6 3 M 1 7 4 F 0.889 8 4 M 0.941 9 5 F 0.833 10 5 M 0.941 # ℹ 26 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Why are tidy data useful? Easy to calculate the `total` and `percent` correct for each student . . . ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 35 × 3 stu_name score_total score_pct 1 Adam 7 39 2 Anne 10 56 3 Audrey 11 61 4 Barbara 6 33 5 Bert 8 44 6 Betty 9 50 7 Blaise 13 72 8 Brenda 10 56 9 Britton 8 44 10 Carol 6 33 # ℹ 25 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Let's try another Are these data tidy? . . . ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 9 sid wave_1_math wave_2_math wave_3_math wave_4_math wave_1_rdg wave_2_rdg 1 1 95 98 102 105 96 98 2 2 101 103 107 109 108 110 3 3 99 103 106 110 103 106 4 4 109 111 115 116 108 109 5 5 101 104 107 113 92 95 # ℹ 2 more variables: wave_3_rdg , wave_4_rdg ``` ::: ::: ## Tidy it! We want separate columns for `wave` and `content` and `score` . . . ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 40 × 4 sid wave content score 1 1 1 math 95 2 1 2 math 98 3 1 3 math 102 4 1 4 math 105 5 1 1 rdg 96 6 1 2 rdg 98 7 1 3 rdg 101 8 1 4 rdg 103 9 2 1 math 101 10 2 2 math 103 # ℹ 30 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Caveats {.smaller} - Tidy data are excellent when conducting preliminary descriptive analyses, plotting data, linear models - Occasionally, you need the data in a different format + if you're using other packages or software for analysis + specific modeling purposes (SEM) + or you have two outcomes variables that might need to be separate column - `math` & `read` . . . ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 10 × 7 id sex ethnicity sped frl math read 1 1 0 5 0 NA 101 99 2 2 1 2 0 NA 96 NA 3 3 1 5 0 NA 131 119 4 4 1 4 0 NA 84 93 5 5 0 1 0 NA 110 118 6 6 0 5 1 NA NA 105 7 7 1 5 1 NA 93 99 8 8 0 3 0 NA 81 77 9 9 1 2 0 NA 129 135 10 10 0 1 0 NA 117 122 ``` ::: ::: ## Tidy Data Made "Simple" 1. Keep each dataset in its own tabular format 2. Put each variable in a column ## Don’t get discouraged! It’s hard to understand tidy principles unless you spend a lot of time working with data Data is often organised to make **data entry** as easy as possible ::: {.incremental} * Tidying is tricky! * Takes practice! * Takes trial and error! * Takes learning and re-learning - a lot! * Takes trial and error! * But you are ~~rarely~~ never gifted with tidy data! ::: ## Some tidy reading suggestions - [*Tidy Data*. Wickham (2014)](http://www.jstatsoft.org/v59/i10/paper) - [R4DS(2e) Chapter 12](https://r4ds.had.co.nz/tidy-data.html) - [R Ladies Sydney: Clean It Up](https://rladiessydney.org/courses/02-cleanitup-0) - [Vignettes](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/articles/pivot.html) ## ![](https://cdn.myportfolio.com/45214904-6a61-4e23-98d6-b140f8654a40/40488240-4609-4dc3-8920-693e078b55ce_rw_1920.jpg?h=2e96a7e21e19c43867546498da026649) ::: aside Credit [Allison Horst](https://allisonhorst.com/data-science-art) ::: # Naming Stuff ## Column Naming Rules **Do use** - lowercase - prefixes and suffixes! + `basc_score`, `basc_date`... + `school_name`, `school_id`, `school_location`... - underscores "`_`" ## Column Naming - A shortened representation of the variable - All variable names must be unique ::: {.incremental} ## Column name examples [prefix]{style='color:#D55E00'}_[name]{style='color:#0072B2'} [id]{style='color:#D55E00'}_[student]{style='color:#0072B2'} [id]{style='color:#D55E00'}_[school]{style='color:#0072B2'} [id]{style='color:#D55E00'}_[district]{style='color:#0072B2'} [surveyID_]{style='color:#D55E00'}[itemID]{style='color:#0072B2'} [sdq_]{style='color:#D55E00'}[25]{style='color:#0072B2'} [survey_]{style='color:#D55E00'}[time_]{style='color:#009E73'}[itemid]{style='color:#0072B2'} [sdq_]{style='color:#D55E00'}[y1_]{style='color:#009E73'}[25]{style='color:#0072B2'} ::: ## Column Naming Rules **Do NOT use** - CAPS - spaces - numbers to start - special characters + **except** underscores "`_`" ## Data Values - **Don't** use numbers for labels! + 0 == "yes" + 1 == "no" - Just use the values! + "never" + "rarely" + "sometimes" + "often" ## Folder & File Naming Rules **Do use** - lowercase - underscores "`_`" or hyphens "`-`" ## Folder & File Naming Rules **Do NOT use** - CAPS - spaces! - special characters + no periods, no slashes! + **except** underscores "`_`" or hyphens "`-`" # Some things I liked from [these slides](https://figshare.com/articles/presentation/Data_Management_and_Data_Management_Plans/7890827?file=14698892) from Jessica Logan ## Document Everything! - It’s so hard to remember what you measured, when you measured it, or why you measured it - Your best strategy is organization and detail + well-documented protocol + a good codebook + data dictionary (documentation of what your variable names mean) - Future you won’t remember what current you decides to do today, or why you decided to do it - Think about someone else using your data later, and what they will need to know ## Misc - Back up your data - Avoid manually-entered questions # Submitted Questions ## Questions {.smaller} ::: {.incremental} 1. *What data management tools do we have access to through UO which typically have a paywall?* - What are you looking for? - [Explore what is available](https://software.uoregon.edu/): https://software.uoregon.edu/ 2. *How can we request data management tools such as Box from UO?* - You can submit a [request](https://service.uoregon.edu/TDClient/2030/Portal/KB/ArticleDet?ID=68409) 3. *Using cloud-based programs such as Dedoose for storing data (example): Advised to also save back-up in OneDrive/elsewhere?* - GitHub is a nice place to store data - UO also has servers - Dropbox? Google Drive? 4. *What are the most novel AND useful data management tools overall?* - R? ::: # Other Questions? ## Let's `pivot_longer()` {visibility="hidden"} Necessary arguments * `data` - of course * `cols` – which columns you will pivot longer * `names_to` – new variable name (in quotes) for those `cols` * `values_to` – new variable name (in quotes) for the cell values ## Let's `pivot_longer()` {visibility="hidden"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} relig_income %>% pivot_longer( cols = _____, names_to = "_____", values_to = "_____" ) ``` ::: . . . ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 18 × 11 religion `<$10k` `$10-20k` `$20-30k` `$30-40k` `$40-50k` `$50-75k` `$75-100k` 1 Agnostic 27 34 60 81 76 137 122 2 Atheist 12 27 37 52 35 70 73 3 Buddhist 27 21 30 34 33 58 62 4 Catholic 418 617 732 670 638 1116 949 5 Don’t k… 15 14 15 11 10 35 21 6 Evangel… 575 869 1064 982 881 1486 949 7 Hindu 1 9 7 9 11 34 47 8 Histori… 228 244 236 238 197 223 131 9 Jehovah… 20 27 24 24 21 30 15 10 Jewish 19 19 25 25 30 95 69 11 Mainlin… 289 495 619 655 651 1107 939 12 Mormon 29 40 48 51 56 112 85 13 Muslim 6 7 9 10 9 23 16 14 Orthodox 13 17 23 32 32 47 38 15 Other C… 9 7 11 13 13 14 18 16 Other F… 20 33 40 46 49 63 46 17 Other W… 5 2 3 4 2 7 3 18 Unaffil… 217 299 374 365 341 528 407 # ℹ 3 more variables: `$100-150k` , `>150k` , # `Don't know/refused` ``` ::: ::: ## Let's `pivot_longer()` {visibility="hidden"} Which `cols` do we want to pivot? <script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
